lead: Every question here gives you a situation and a clock: a crew in the water, smoke, a lee shore four cables off. Know the first action, and work out how long you have.

blocks.p: Prevention first. The skipper may be the casualty, so every crew member must know the drill.

fig.title: Before a night passage
lines: Everyone can send the DSC alert, not only you
Clip on before the hatch, then to the jackstay
Lifejacket indicator red: re-arm before use
Seasick crew: cockpit, clipped on, watched
Seasickness pills hours before sailing
Raft: room for everyone, service in date

fig.title: Man overboard
lines: Shout · throw the danbuoy and lifebuoy
Press MOB now: 3 min at 6 kn is 0.3 M late
One pointer, who does nothing else
Out of sight or dark: DSC alert, MAYDAY
Spinnaker up: get it down, then turn back
Before the engine: no lines in the water

blocks.p: Under sail, the **quick-stop** tacks at once with the jib left sheeted, so she stops nearby; reach-turn-reach sails off on a beam reach, tacks and returns. Approach on a **close reach**, where letting the sheets fly stops her.

fig.note: Close reach: ease the sheets and she stops

blocks.p: The MOB waypoint is fixed to the ground; he drifts with the stream. A danbuoy blows downwind faster than a swimmer: search **upwind** of it. His AIS beacon shows on your plotter; a PLB, held high, aerial upright, calls the rescue centre by satellite.

sections.title: Lift him level, warm him gently

blocks.p: **Cold shock** makes him gasp in water in the first minute; a sprayhood protects the airway. After long immersion lift him **level**, in two strops on a halyard or rolled in a sail: a vertical lift can cause collapse. At a stern ladder, or a catamaran's stern steps, **stop that engine** first; never bring him between the hulls.

head: Casualty
What you do
rows: Dry clothes, insulation, warm sweet drinks
Flat, gentle handling, insulation; no drinks
Five rescue breaths, then CPR 30:2; MAYDAY
Medical advice: trouble can follow hours later
Cool water 20 min, then loose cling film
Splint as found, sling, check fingers
Sips of rehydration fluid; medical advice

fig.title: Before you call for medical advice
lines: Pulse, breathing, temperature
What happened, and when
Medicines already given
What is in your first-aid kit
Your position and ETA

blocks.p: Tired and seasick? Anchor, rest, and enter by daylight.

sections.title: Fuel, air or heat: take one away

head: Fire
First action
rows: Fire blanket, gas off; never water
Stop engine and fuel; extinguisher through the fire port
Batteries off, then CO2 or powder; never water
Water or foam, to cool it

lines: Smoke from the engine box
Opening it feeds the fire: use the fire port

blocks.p: Keep an extinguisher **by each exit**, to fight with the way out behind you.

**LPG** is heavier than air and sinks into the bilge, so the alarm sensor sits low and one spark is enough. Headache, drowsiness and nausea in a closed cabin with the heater or engine running mean **carbon monoxide**: everyone into fresh air.

fig.title: Smell of gas
lines: Shut it off at the cylinder
Touch no switch: a spark ignites it
Open up and ventilate
Pump the bilge with the hand pump
Find leaks with soapy water, never a flame

blocks.p: After a collision, grounding or lightning strike, check the crew, then look for water: lightning can blow out a through-hull. In a thunderstorm keep the crew below, clear of the mast, with a spare handheld VHF and GPS in the oven.

Water below: pump **and** hunt. Fresh water with the pressure pump running by itself is your own tank; salt means seacocks, hoses, stern gland. A sheared seacock takes the softwood **bung** tied beside it. Holed in the port bow, sail on port tack: she heels to starboard and lifts the hole.

fig.title: Can the pumps keep up?
lines: Inflow about 70 L/min
Electric pump: 30 L/min
Manual: 0.6 L × 45 strokes = 27 L/min
Engine intake hose in the bilge: 40 L/min
Out 97 − in 70 = 27 L/min in hand

fig.title: Aground
lines: Tide falling: astern at once, along your track
Crew out on the boom to heel her
Holed on a rock: stem the leak and call
before the rising tide floats her off

fig.note: Bank slopes down to the east · pad her bilge

blocks.p: Steering gone: stop or heave to, then ship the **emergency tiller**. Try it once in harbour first.

sections.title: Distance ÷ drift is the time you have

blocks.cap: 0.4 M ÷ 1.2 kn = 20 minutes: anchor now, then call PAN-PAN.

blocks.p: With 40 minutes and sails ready, hoist and claw off instead. Disabled in a shipping lane: **PAN-PAN** to ships and the VTS. Dragging onto rocks half an hour away: **MAYDAY**. Take a tow on a bridle round strong points, led over the bow roller.

Before a gale reef and rig the storm jib early, and head offshore: a bar breaks in an onshore blow. Ride it out **hove to**, or run off with a **drogue** holding her stern to the seas. Never lie a-hull: beam-on, a breaking crest rolls her.

fig.note: Hove to: jib aback, main eased, tiller to leeward

fig.title: How long does the sea room last?
lines: A gale for 10 h, 30 M of sea room:
bare poles 5 kn = 50 M · hove to 1.5 kn = 15 M
A gale for 6 h, 21 M of sea room:
running at 7 kn it lasts 3 h;
with a drogue at 2.5 kn, 8 h 24 min

sections.title: Alert by DSC, then speak on 16

blocks.p: **MAYDAY** means grave and imminent danger to the vessel or a person; **SÉCURITÉ** warns of a hazard, such as a container awash. Send the DSC alert even with no position on the set, then give it by voice on 16.

fig.title: MAYDAY on 16
lines: MAYDAY ×3 · THIS IS Selene ×3
MAYDAY Selene, call sign, MMSI
Position: 220°T from the light, 4.0 M
Nature of distress · help needed
Persons aboard · other information
OVER

fig.note: 043°M − 3°W = 040°T to the light · you: 220°T from it

blocks.p: Do not acknowledge another vessel's alert by DSC: listen on 16 and, if no coast station answers, acknowledge by voice. SEELONCE MAYDAY keeps you off 16 until SEELONCE FEENEE. Cancel a false alert on the set, then tell all stations.

fig.note: Silent radio: note bearing and time, MAYDAY RELAY

head: Flare
Use
rows: Far from help; under low cloud, 45° downwind
Help in sight at night; hold it downwind

blocks.p: A coast station hears VHF only in **sea area A1**; beyond it, ships nearby and the EPIRB. To be seen, hoist the radar reflector high in the catch-rain position and fit an AIS **transponder**, not just a receiver.

fig.title: How far does your VHF reach?
lines: Range ≈ 2.2 × (√h1 + √h2) M, h in metres
Masthead 16 m, station 81 m: 28.6 M
Dismasted, aerial at 4 m: 2.2 × 11 = 24.2 M
A1: some 20–30 M from a coast station
70 M crossing, 25 M each side: 20 M outside

blocks.p: A sound hull is bigger, warmer and easier to find than a raft: dismasted but dry, you stay. Call early, but leave only when she is sinking or burning.

fig.title: Into the raft
lines: Painter made fast to the yacht first
Launch to leeward · on fire: to windward
Pull the painter to inflate; step in dry
Take grab bag, EPIRB, water, warm clothes
Cut the painter, get clear, stream the drogue
EPIRB stays on · SART high on its pole

blocks.p: A raft upside down: stand on the gas-bottle side and lean back on the righting strap. In a deck cradle a **hydrostatic release** frees it a few metres down. A **SART** paints 12 dots on a searching radar; the nearest marks the raft. A capsized catamaran floats: stay with it.

fig.title: Helicopter
lines: Stow the bimini and loose gear: downwash
The pilot briefs you on 16: course, speed
Let the hi-line touch the sea first
Take it in by hand · never make it fast
The lift may be from the dinghy, towed astern
